title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 5: Q&A on the Comelec Leadership
keywords: enforce and administer all election laws
the unexpired balance of the term
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's October 14, 2007 Inquirer column, a Q&A on Comelec leadership following his call to 'energize' the poll body to 'finally reform and automate our archaic election system' and hold 'credible, speedy and peaceful elections'

His answer that, forced to choose, a 'visionary leader' beats a 'great lawyer' as Comelec chair -- because the Comelec must 'enforce and administer' election laws, needing 'innovative leadership, executive ability, and InfoTech know-how' (the President need not even be a lawyer), with election-law expertise supplied by the commissioners (as the Monsod precedent showed)

Why the Constitution bans Comelec reappointments and limits appointees to the predecessor's 'unexpired balance' (Gaminde v. COA) -- both to preserve the staggered 'two-year interval' and the poll body's independence from a President who normally serves six years (though GMA, by a 'constitutional quirk,' could appoint all seven)

His view that GMA was 'ill advised' to propose postponing the October 2007 barangay elections, citing David v. Comelec's rebuke of 'self-serving propositions to lengthen governance without a mandate from the governed' -- a postponement the Senate wisely scuttled
sub_topics: Leader or jurist?: asked whether a 'great lawyer who is a so-so leader' or a 'visionary leader who is not so great a lawyer' makes the better Comelec chair, CJP picks the latter -- the Comelec needs 'a leader (not just a manager)' who pursues a clear vision and models 'integrity, independence, transparency, accountability, probity, and competence'

Why leadership over law: the Comelec is mandated to 'enforce and administer' election laws, which demands 'innovative leadership, executive ability, and InfoTech know-how,' not chiefly 'legal skills' -- just as 'the chief executive of our country, the president, is not even required to be a lawyer' (his earlier column was titled 'Choosing credible Comelec leaders,' not 'jurists')

Where the law comes in: as the President is aided by the justice secretary, presidential legal counsel and solicitor general, so the Comelec chair should be 'complemented by commissioners who are well versed in election law' for the body's judicial functions

The Monsod precedent: when Christian Monsod's credentials were challenged for not 'actively' practicing law, the Court liberally read 'practice of law' to count his 'legal management experience' -- a 'hairline 8-to-7 decision' vindicated when Monsod (with commissioners like Haydee Yorac) ran 'honest, orderly, and peaceful elections'

The reappointment ban: the prohibition (to the same post or the chairmanship) is 'designed to assure the independence and integrity of the Comelec,' since commissioners hoping for reappointment or promotion are 'vulnerable to the partisan wiles' of the appointing President and the confirming Commission on Appointments

The 'unexpired balance' rule: per Gaminde v. Commission on Audit (Dec. 13, 2000), an appointee serves only the predecessor's 'unexpired balance of the term' to keep the constitutionally designed 'two-year interval between the expiration of terms' (the first seven commissioners holding 7-, 5- and 3-year terms, then 7 years each)

Why the stagger matters -- and the GMA exception: the interval keeps a President (normally six years) from appointing all seven commissioners, safeguarding independence -- but GMA, by a 'constitutional quirk,' could serve about nine and a half years (3.5 as Estrada's successor plus six as elected President) and thus appoint all seven

The barangay-postponement coda: CJP calls GMA 'ill advised' to propose moving the October 29, 2007 barangay elections to August 2008, invoking David v. Comelec (1997), which struck down deferral petitions as 'self-serving propositions to lengthen governance without a mandate from the governed' -- noting it would overage the 2002 Sangguniang Kabataan and waste the Comelec's spending, so by scuttling it 'the Senate may have saved GMA from another splitting legal headache'

stances.claim: Forced to choose, a 'visionary leader' makes a better Comelec chair than a 'great lawyer,' because the body must 'enforce and administer' election laws (needing executive and InfoTech leadership), with election-law expertise supplied by the commissioners -- as the Monsod precedent vindicated.
stances.rhetorical_move: prioritization with precedent: ranking leadership over legal credentials and proving it by example

stances.claim: The reappointment ban and the 'unexpired balance' rule (Gaminde) both exist to protect the Comelec's independence -- keeping commissioners from currying favor for reappointment and stopping any one President from appointing all seven, an aim defeated only by GMA's 'constitutional quirk.'
stances.rhetorical_move: design-rationale explanation: tying two technical rules to the single value of independence

stances.claim: Postponing the barangay elections was an 'ill advised' bid to 'lengthen governance without a mandate from the governed' (David v. Comelec), so the Senate's refusal to allow it 'saved GMA from another splitting legal headache.'
stances.rhetorical_move: precedent-backed rebuke: condemning the postponement with a prior ruling and a wry coda

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's October 14, 2007 Inquirer column, is a Q&A on Comelec leadership prompted by his call to 'energize' the poll body to 'finally reform and automate our archaic election system' and hold 'credible, speedy and peaceful elections.' Asked whether a 'great lawyer who is a so-so leader' or a 'visionary leader who is not so great a lawyer' would make the better chair, he picks the latter: the Comelec must 'enforce and administer' election laws, which demands 'innovative leadership, executive ability, and InfoTech know-how' rather than chiefly legal skill -- 'the president... is not even required to be a lawyer' -- with election-law expertise supplied by the commissioners. He cites the Monsod precedent, where the Court liberally read 'practice of law' to qualify Christian Monsod on his 'legal management experience' (a 'hairline 8-to-7 decision' vindicated by 'honest, orderly, and peaceful elections'). He then explains two independence-protecting rules: the ban on reappointments (lest commissioners curry favor with the appointing President and the confirming Commission on Appointments) and the 'unexpired balance of the term' rule from Gaminde v. COA (2000), which preserves the staggered 'two-year interval' so no single President -- normally serving six years -- can appoint all seven, an aim defeated only by GMA's 'constitutional quirk' of about nine and a half years. Finally, he faults GMA's 'ill advised' proposal to postpone the October 2007 barangay elections, invoking David v. Comelec (1997) against 'self-serving propositions to lengthen governance without a mandate from the governed,' and notes that by scuttling the move 'the Senate may have saved GMA from another splitting legal headache.'
